summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
Per GAO, Twenty of 23 federal agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of the reported use cases were in the planning phase and not yet in production; in about 200 instances, agencies reported that they were currently using AI. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases.

GAO lists what agencies use AI for: analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers. Some agencies are also using AI operationally to identify information security threats and facilitate the review of large datasets. The same audit found that agency inventories had incomplete and inaccurate data: five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, and two inventories included AI uses later determined by the agencies to not be AI.

On money and implementation, the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI, per GAO. Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA established the AI Center of Excellence, and those two agencies fully implemented selected requirements. OMB has not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, and OPM has not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work. Ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt from the requirements.

Stanford HAI's AI Index reports a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it, with frameworks to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology falling behind and data transparency declining. OECD.AI gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives and works on transparency and comparability of risk mitigation measures. Oxford Insights ranks national readiness on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption. The AI Laws tracker on theworldofai.org, updated daily from LegiScan, tracks 5,932 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions. Its review of 100 measures across 27 states found no two states wrote the same law; only Colorado and Texas passed broad laws reaching consequential decisions across sectors, while every other measure names one setting. Common rules recur: AI may assist, but it may not be the only decider in personal stakes, insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone, AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician, and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. No state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law; the attorney general enforces the larger laws, and several states simply declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act.

A reader deciding whether to deploy in government should note that federal adoption is mostly planning, not production, and that GAO found incomplete and inaccurate inventories, no government-wide acquisition guidance, and unmet requirements. The state patchwork means the question is never whether you use AI but what you use it for, per the AI Laws tracker. The common core to build to: tell people when they are dealing with AI, keep a qualified person in any decision about health, employment, benefits, or education, have a crisis protocol and know the age of your user if the product holds a conversation, and keep records of what the system does. The sources do not quantify returns on investment; GAO frames benefits as potential and says agencies cannot effectively address AI risks and benefits until all requirements are met.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI is a policy observatory that maintains a database of over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, alongside live AI data and policy analysis. The platform promotes the OECD AI Principles to help countries develop trustworthy AI systems, and invites organisations developing advanced AI to submit reports on their risk mitigation measures to improve transparency and comparability. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative merged with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand to form an integrated partnership. The observatory aims to support AI actors in building systems that respect human rights, fairness, transparency, explainability, robustness, and security.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page reports tracking 5,932 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily from LegiScan, and compares 100 enacted measures across 27 states as of September 18, 2026. It notes that no two states wrote the same law, and only Colorado and Texas passed broad laws covering consequential decisions across sectors, while other measures target specific settings. A recurring rule is that AI may assist but cannot be the sole decider in personal matters, such as insurers denying care on an algorithm alone or AI delivering therapy. The page states no state created a new enforcement agency; attorneys general enforce the larger laws, and some states treat violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices. It advises building to common duties like disclosing AI use, keeping a qualified person in health, employment, benefits, or education decisions, and keeping records because the attorney general is the most likely enforcer.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
